posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body:
I said "wow this thread is going to go over well" when I saw it, and was not disappointed.
Anyhow, here's some things about RM that get under my skin:
* The majority of the Olivia Octopath plugin set. I'm not fond of them due to how clunky they are, for starters. The turn order plugin particular I find very ugly and unintuitive, and given that it seems to be a perfect recreation of the order indicator from Octopath that's not exactly a good thing. It's also that I've seen people use it and the boost system out of the box, and each time it's been like: "Why would I play this instead of the real Octopath?"
* Kinda sick to death of seeing generic anime-medieval setting games in this engine. If you're gonna throw a medieval world at me, give me one with actual culture that isn't just the isekai starter pack.
* Not using unique SFX. I swear to Christ if I hear Flash2 at 150 pitch in a game with fully custom art, my hair will fall out. Dramatics aside, I do find it to be a shame when people neglect sound design because that's a significant part of your game's soul other than how it looks.
* The fact there's only four sound channels.
I'd say more if I could remember more things I disliked.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
My hot takes:
1.  The vast majority of the gamedevs who use the program know nothing about gamedev and most don't care to learn.  You can quickly and easily tell when you let a dev know that the thing they are doing might cause problems or has inherent disadvantages... and instead of saying, "I know, here's what I'm doing to make sure those aren't problems" they say something along the lines of, "It's my vision", "It's not actually a problem", or "I don't care about how many people will play game, it's for a very specific niche audience of just me, and anyone who thinks like me".  This is how you can tell the difference between users who care about the craft, and those just wanting quick fame/fortune/recognition.  One of these people wants to do the best they possibly can, no matter how large the workload.  The other of these people wants to create "minimum viable product".
2.  Too many people use plugins to accomplish things, rather than learning how to event it.  Plugins are incredibly useful for a variety of things, but then you get people requesting plugins for easy to code stuff, or installing plugins that you could quickly event yourself.  There's a massive over-reliance on everyone else doing the work for you.
3.  The 1 tile large sprites suck.  I want to go back to the 1.5 tile high sprites of older makers.  They are far superior.
4.  There's a lot of misinformation perpetuated on this site regarding game design and even gamer preferences.  Just as an example:  "The RTP is bad and anyone who uses it is lazy".  Or "On Screen Encounters are superior.".  All of this stuff is "situational".  Good game devs realize this.  Or, they just couch it in "just my opinion" instead.  "I don't like the way the RTP looks", "I prefer to have the encounters on screen because...".
5.  People are weird for trying to turn RPG Maker into games that aren't RPG's.  Like... you do realize you can get a program like "Game Maker" instead, if you want to make a platformer, right?  You do realize that it's near impossible to make a horror game from the top down perspective, right?  I have no idea why you're using RPG Maker to create a 3rd person shooter.  There are better engines on the market for these types of games, why choose RPG Maker for it?  It baffles me.
6.  It's ridiculous that we have so little control over the engine without plugins.  What if I want to create some "running shoes" from Final Fantasy 6?  Good luck doing that very easily, or at all, without a plugin.
7.  The RTP Library isn't large enough and there aren't enough DLC options for getting more of it.  Why are we missing wolves and bears?  I think each base engine should come with at minimum, 300 monsters to work with.  Even 200 would be good.
8.  Too many devs of this program are super invested in "designing things backwards".  Rather than creating a piece of equipment that is appropriate for the Quest Reward, they create the piece of equipment and then try to create a Quest that feels "appropriate" to the power of the eqiupment.  It's like this all over in this community, not just Quest design.
9.  It's insane how many people design a game "to work", rather than "for fun".  If you ask a dev "Yeah, but is that fun?" they don't have a proper answer.  Ask, "what about that is fun?" and watch their brains short-circuit.  It's all "I played a game that was fun, that had this in it, so if I put this thing in my game, it automatically makes my game fun!".  "Rule of cool" only works if what you have designed actually is cool.  Not "it was cool in this other game I played".
10.  RPG Maker games end up being bad usually because almost all devs are amateur ones.  Not because there's anything inherently wrong with the engine or default assets.  Heavily overdesigned and artworked games can be (and often are), just as awful to play as the ones that aren't.  It works just like AAA games these days.  Sure, you poured a lot of resources into your game, but you're still an amateur, who made a bad game.  A bad game is a bad game.  It can be covered in poo or it can be gold plated poo that smells of roses.  Still poo at the end of the day.  You want to make a good game, you test play it a lot.  You make sure people are having fun with the game.  The point of a game is TO BE FUN.  If it is not fun, you are not designing a game.  You're designing a series of systems.
11.  There's a lot of "gamez r art" people in this community than there are in others, or even among actual gamers.  It's easiest to just mentally mark these people's opinion on any art as invalid since they have no idea what "art" even is.  If you've seen "The Menu", you've seen what these people are.  They're "Tyler".  If you are making a game as some kind of "statement", then I'm sorry, but you aren't a creative.  You're a poser.

Just speaking on the "buyers and sellers" argument side of things here.  I've got a new Hot Take.
Honestly, everyone who buys/sells things for RPG Maker (or, in general, really), needs to be extremely familiar with The Rules of Acquisition.  A person who is a bad business person reads them as "exploitative".  A person who is a good business person sees them as "Advice for how to deal with any transaction in your life, and your business".
There's a reason "caveat emptor" exists as a phrase.  By and large, people will charge what they can get people to pay for something.  If I can charge you $100 for a mediocre cut of steak with gold leaf on it, and you pay for it... that's not exploitative.  That is "the customer finds that price to be acceptable, for whatever reason they want to find it acceptable".
If the price of something is "not what you're willing to pay", then you just don't pay for it.  If a LOT of people decide they aren't willing to pay that for it, then the person trying to sell it usually goes out of business, unless they still make enough sales to meet their overhead and a bit of profit to live on.
Just as an easy example:
Switch 2 - $500.
Why does an inferior quality machine cost the same as my Xbox?  I'm not buying a Switch 2 at that price.
Other people, however, found the purchase "to be worth it".  So, they bought it.  $500 was perfectly reasonable to those people.
Heck, if consumers really cared so much about "predatory business practices", we wouldn't have ever had loot crates and gacha systems to begin with.  Microtransactions wouldn't have been a thing.  But they are.  They were.  Because they make money.
Unfortunately, that's just how business works.  If you can't afford it or don't think the price is worth it, you don't pay for it.  Or, you negotiate.  I know plenty of artists who are willing to negotiate prices for things.
Or... does nobody haggle anymore?  Like... that is my favorite part of being a merchant in any MMO (or Dungeons and Dragons).  Haggling.  Making deals.  It seems like nobody even tries that anymore.  They just accept whatever price someone puts forth.  Everyone just acts like someone is out to take advantage of them when they get haggled with.
Like, the art of trading is two people have things the other wants.  How do they come to an agreement to get those things?  I'm unable to pay more than $X for a product.  Can you come up with a way for me to still get that product, or no?  No?  Okay, I'll go elsewhere.  Yes?  Okay, how?  Payment plan?  Financing?  Do I need to throw in collateral?  Offer something else alongside the cash to make up the difference?
Anyway:
Rule of Acquisition #3:  Never spend more for an acquision than you have to.
Rule of Acquisition #22:  Wise men can hear profit on the wind.
Rule of Acquisition #47:  Don't trust a man wearing a better suit than your own.
Rule of Acquisition #59:  Free advice is seldom cheap.
Rule of Acquisition #98:  Every man has his price.

The second half of this thread was terrible to read so I propose we move on and go back on saying actual hot takes. Here's mine:
• RPG Maker should go back on being drastically different from one release to the other. XP did not invalidate 2K3 because they're different and allow different things. The SV enemies are just the FV enemies but sometimes flipped, really? I could have done it myself at that point. If you intend to have different artwork for front and side view, at least make them different. Currently the RTP enemies suck even if you like the art style because they all either look too much on the side for a front view battle or too much on the front for a side view battle, I want the enemy to look at the party, not somewhere else in the distance.
• Variable managing is awful to the point that I still use VXA for a specific script that exist only for Ace that, among other things, allow actual
decent
variable managing. There is no float, no array, no self variables. Do you want me to use global variable each time I need to count something specific to one event? And how is there no native management of another event's self switches? I don't want to use a global switch for trivial things such as two characters disappearing but for larger scales things such as "did the player accomplish X side quest?" or "did the player activate X mecanism earlier?" type of things that actually impact other parts of the game (for example a NPC lowering it price if you accomplish X side quest or a door being opened early if you already activated X mecanism)

For real, people see side-view battles (ATB optional) as shout: "OMG it's like FF on the NES and SNES!"
But Final Fantasy I to VI aren't just side-view battles and pixel art.
It's also recurring spells, like Cura, Firaga, Esuna, and Ultima.
It's also recurring Jobs, like Red Mage, Blue Mage, Summoner, and Geomancer.
It's also recurring monsters, like the Cactuar, the Malboro, the mid-game Flan, the Adamantoise, and D&D's compendium.
It's also Chocobos and Cid and Airships and Gil and plot-relevent crystals in a setting that isn't purely medieval fantasy (seriously, even the first game had a futuristic fortress with a bipedal mecha as a super tough enemy) and magic mixed with technology.
It's also mechanics generally not seen in other RPGs, like a Ninja who throws weapons, a knife empowered by running away, a Death spell that kills everything whose level is a multiple of 5, and healing based on the user's HP.
Final Fantasy isn't all these things at once, but its identity is tied to having multiple of these recurring elements in one place.

Afterall, I think the best part of RPG Maker is the community and their ability help each other out which I believe came from a necessity of features that were wanted but not offered in the core scripts. Leading to the RPG Maker community having a bunch of smart people who are also familiar with the engine and are able to help you anytime of the day and a bunch of them making hundreds of FREE plugins that solves most people's problems anyways. Those experienced developers would've never gotten into coding if they had everything they wanted and more. So I want to thank GGG for torturing them with the curse of knowledge. Plus, I have like zero expectations for any big corporation anyways so it's not much of a loss to me if they don't do anything.
Furthermore, RPG Maker was made to be a template, even if it's half-filled with mechanics already, it was made with the intent to be overwritten. So plugins are a must have, both for the developer and player experience (not every game needs plugins but a lot rely on them). I do love how Dark Souls has several alternating menus that show the lore, stats, and stat differences and I do think most JRPGs would benefit from having stat differences being shown as a standard, but setting that as a standard feature could be dangerous. Afterall, why stop at stat differences? Let's add in timed parrying and dodging since Clair Obscure had it and it's clearly the populace choice. But not every game benefits from features that everyone wants, a horror game might benefit from having limited combat options or even limited menu information, getting rid of displaying stats could be a standard feature for horror games who knows. It's much better to have modularized plugins for those that need them than to have a universal feature than requires a plugin to remove and potentially causes bugs and plugin compatibility issues. And I wouldn't be complaining if GGG adds those features in a plugin but they be selling their plugins upwards to 50$ GODDAMN.
Additionally, I just like having fun implementing mini plugins even for basic things like altering the formula for dodging and I do admire how
most
of the code is super clean, readable, and modifiable. And I even have fun for the big and confusing plugins as I feel a sense of accomplishment for making something that complex even if I feel frustrated most of the time. So I'd rather have GGG just focus on optimizations and QoL features like a UI editor than adding new game mechanics that bloat up or conflict with existing plugins entirely. But I do understand that keeping a lot of those features locked behind plugins do scare those unfamiliar with coding and does put a skill wall to implementing features. But that's where the smart people in the community come in to help and communicate with you even for the most niche of things.
I'd rather have a passionate RPG Maker community than a company that would take 10 business years to implement a single feature in.
My only rebuttal being that having a community like this could lead to GGG being complacent like Bethesda and releasing buggy software after buggy software and just having a downward slope in overall quality, I blame Todd Howard. Really wish you can have a good modding community and a company that listens but there are no wishes made without a monkey paw's finger curling.
Edit: AND BEFORE ANYONE SAYS "If you want modularity so much than just work in Godot or Unity or make your own engine" I WILL MARRY YOUR MOTHER AND HAVE A HAPPY LIFE WITH HER. I ALREADY TRIED MAKING TILE BASED MOVEMENT IN GAME MAKER AND FAILED. I'm just saying that I think RPG Maker MZ is
mostly
fine as it is now, needling the thread for being a RPG framework while being used for lots of other genres as well and being super modifiable would be a hard task to accomplish and GGG balances it fairly well IMO.

If you're going commercial (unless you're doing a web or mobile first game) Steam is pretty much an absolute must. No other platform gets the traffic and subsequently sales that Steam does, especially for indies.  Consoles have a higher barrier to entry and more requirements to even get on their store and will not bring the same level of sales Steam will for the extra effort required to support them.
As for graphics vs writing. Video games are a visual medium at the end of the day. The thumbnail is what catches someone's eye and causes them to click through to your product page. Then they will look at your screenshots, then trailer. All visual heavy. The blurb/short description of your game needs to convey what type of game it is first and foremost, with lore as secondary. People get invested in lore AFTER they've downloaded and started playing your game, not before. The more narrative-oriented your game is the more story will matter, for some game genres story can be non existent and not matter.
BTW, the cover is the #1 selling point for books too. Publish a book without a cover and see how many sales it gets.

If being told what you made sucks, demotivates you... you're not really that much of a creative to begin with.  You're in it for the recognition, not "the love of the game".
Now, I'm not saying it's easy to let that kind of thing roll off your back.  It isn't.  Because most people who make a think put a piece of themselves into it, so being told it sucks is the equivalent of being told that YOU suck, personally.

That's sort of what it means to create.  You don't do it for the recognition.  Or the accolades.  Or the hope someone will understand you and the work.  You do it, because your SOUL needs to do it. Samolexie said:
Now about the game having a soul, 80% of the time, when people talk about such things, they talk about games with high quality custom graphics that fits the tone of the story, etc
Click to expand...
That's because graphics are what you see what you get type of deal when things like writing and mechanics have to be mentally invested in to fully understand and appreciated. But good art does not cover up for any poor game mechanics or writing in general. And high quality graphics DO have a soul because in order to reach that quality an artists takes tens of thousands of hours to perfect their art, in the process, creating their own artistic expression. The same applies to any creative work and people will praise you for excelling in any one area.
Take for example, Undertale/Deltarune (not talking about the early fandom they were all weirdos) everyone talks about how compelling the characters are more than how good looking the sprites because Toby Fox is a master of characterization and interactions (plus music). And while Temmie Chang is a skilled artist it's that Tricky Tony just outshines her in pure writing prowess. You don't need god-tier art, just characters to invest in and love (SUSIE NUMBERO 1#####).
Another example, Ultrakill, literally only YouTube essayists care about the lore and everyone plays for the music and Ultrafast gameplay. But it just shows you only need to excel one or two areas to show your game has a soul because people, whether consciously or not, know that these creative works and skills take thousands of frustrating errors to correct. And perseverance is one of humanities' most defining traits that people crowd around.
It's a natural thing to trip and fall and have people laugh at you but at the end of the day YOU took the steps to become better. And those who have succeeded have been in your exact circumstances, they're just went from tripping to winning marathons. But even now those popular creators/writers (mostly mangakas) still receive death threats even if their works are objectively good, so people will always complain no matter how good your writing is. So don't write for an audience, write for yourself, the audience will find you (but do stay aware your writing will be read by other people because I hate when authors skimp over details because it's already envisioned in their head, leaving me confused on what's happening).
The thing about game making is that it's an interdisciplinary work, meaning you need several skills to make one (depending on the genre) or find someone else who does have those skills. So the amount of times you WILL stumble increases multiplicatively, or even exponentially depending on how everything meshes together. But that's why games are so wonderful, better than books or movies or anything. Because a game can become any of those or more. It just relies on the powers of the developer to bring their imagination into reality. I want to read, experience, and fall in love with something that a developer has summoned forth through sheer will power alone, even against all odds of giving up. Someone who has worked hard to carve a soul out of nothing, taken their time understanding why every trope works and when/how to break them, made countless errors and experimentations is much more compelling than anyone who is naturally talented. And that's why you shouldn't be discouraged even if your first game does suck balls.
Edit: I forgot to glaze Fear and Hunger.
Another thing about game making is that even if you write the next bible your work could go underground for potentially forever. Fear and Hunger only became popular after YouTubers made videos about it despite it being released years earlier IIRC. I never made tutorials for the RPG Maker, but I did use to push the "Training Game" format.  A way to "self learn" what things do and how to do them.
If I remember right, what I would tell newbies to do is create like a "door opening puzzle" using 3 switches.  It's a pretty good way to learn how variables work, trying to design a puzzle like that.  Especially if you have like 8 doors that open/close based on the switch you use.
You could have one lever "add 1", another lever "subtract 1" and the third lever "divide by 3".  Then, have the puzzle "reset" back to say... 20 when the variable reaches 0 in any way.  Then, the doors can check whether they should be open or closed based on "range".  Maybe they're all closed if you go above 20.  Maybe they all open if you manage to get it to 2.
I think a "Training Game" format works great for teaching new users how things in the engine work.  Just a "here's what your game HAS to have, and how it HAS to work", then the new user has to kind of figure out how to accomplish a lot of the more common things in ways where they can iterate on what they did, rather than just rote memorize what they need.
It isn't enough to teach someone how to use a variable.  You need to teach them how to use it in a way where it clicks and they can think of 5 other things they can do with it, on their own.

Of course, I'm not trying to argue that either. All I'm saying is that because of the similarities and overlaps between solo dev and collaboration, if you can't achieve anything as a solo dev, you likely won't achieve anything by collaborating either.
Let's say for example you can't draw. You can still make a game with RTP, free resources, or your own badly drawn art. Naturally, it's probably not going to be the best or most unique, but it's something. If you can't manage even that, then even if you had an artist to work with, that will not change anything. The artist can only make the game better if it can actually exist to begin with.
Or let's say you can't code. Fortunately, RPG Maker has no programming knowledge required, as well as quite a lot of free plugins. In a sense, the RPG Maker devs and plugin authors have already done the coding for you. Sure, you'll be limited in what you can do with just that. But if you can't make something half-decent within those limitations, I doubt having access to all the additional possibilities you can imagine unlocked via the power of programming will improve anything. In fact, it can even make things worse if you end up scope creeping.
Don't get me wrong, I'm not trying to argue against collaboration. I do agree that it can sometimes be beneficial. But for it to actually work, you need to be able to pull your own weight. And that's something you can learn by being a solo dev. As the age old advice goes, start small.

posts.author: Rethy
posts.body:
It's interesting to see people's differing attitudes towards RTP. I burnt out on drawing but still wanted to make something, so I basically set out to make a game I thought was fun and interesting within the limitations of relying only on the default assets as much as possible.
It's been a marketing question I've wrestled with for a while, knowing that most of the audience for RPG Maker games are other RPG Maker users, how to communicate "The entire point of this game is that it uses the default assets but it is cool and different from all the other games that use default assets" without being disparaging to the other games and creators that use them. One phrase that has stuck with me through development is "We have Motoi Sakuraba at home" and I say that with all the affection in the world.
As for my own hot take, I got beef with Yanfly.
The core engine and battle core are treated like pre-requisites, but they make so many changes to the base engine and then either have their alterations as the default parameters, or even make certain changes without the option to toggle them off. One of the biggest examples is the Battle core is built assuming people are using sideview for battle, so there's tons of changes that mess with the presentation and gameplay feedback if you're using frontview. I downloaded Action Sequence Pack 2, realised it broke some of my windows, so I copied the single line of javascript I needed the plugin for and removed it.
I've lost multiple days of game dev trying to fix or restore something that worked perfectly fine in the base engine. My most recent annoyance was realising the Battle Core doesn't display the State Messages for the KO state in the battlelog, but can't be toggled in the parameters like other messages. I could use the Buffs & States core to add them back manually with <Custom Apply Effect> and <Custom Remove Effect>, but I'd rather the thing that worked perfectly with the core engine just worked like normal, and there's always subtle differences in the behaiour you have to keep you eye out for.

While we're mentioning "enemy hues", I really have a problem with RPG Maker's method of "recoloring" sprites.  The hue shift is nice, but it REALLY needs an option to "customize colors", as it's more difficult to get thematically colored enemies just based on what the default colors are.  RPG Maker desperately needs a "primary", "secondary", and "tertiary" color option change for sprites as well.  Maybe that's too difficult to program, but it doesn't stop the fact that it needs to exist.
Likewise, there isn't really an option to make an enemy "monochrome" either.
Any of that, and you either have to learn to recolor yourself (something I will never be good at) or ask someone else to do it for you.
The problem with advertising RPG Maker as "so easy, anyone can do it" is that it is desperately lacking in many features standard RPG's have, as well as features a basic dev team would be able to do.
This is to say nothing of the really badly programmed animation creation feature in the program as well.  It stumbles hard in the "helping you create decently unique assets with what is here on default".

A big limitation I see with the hue shifts is often when you move something in the green/cyan range, even though number-wise it has the same level of saturation as the default sprite, to the human eye it looks all toxic and blown-out and oversaturated on most sprites.
I don't know if there's a way to add something like color regions while keeping the editor lightweight, but thinking on it now they probably should at least have Saturation/Brightness sliders as well.
I think the two domains where the editor really falls short are battles, and what I'll call "Presentation"- things like color adjustments, animations, menu options, layout and UI, ect. It sort of makes sense in terms of those being two aspects that people are going to have the most varied needs for and be very fiddly if you try to account for what every possible user's every possible needs would be. There should still at least be a page to set some basic values, like dodge chance, crit chance, guard multiplier, and some TP behaviour.
I think the person who said RPG Maker is a game engine for writers a while back was partially right, in that what it gives you out-of-the-box is enough to cover every other decision for you. If you want to customise anything other than the writing and direct sequence of events, you have to roll up your sleeves and do it yourself.

It's OK to use AI. I judge your game by how it plays, not by whatever tools you used to make it.
It's OK to use RTP (assets). However, if you use RTP database skills and items, I'm not giving your game another look.
Interactive art galleries and walking simulators suck, give me an actual game to play, with real gameplay. For every hour you spend making your game look pretty, spend another 10 hours making it fun to play.

This is something I am working on in my game.
I want to create a game that's remembered not just for its story and visuals, but its gameplay as well. I want players to talk not just about my art style or characters, but also my systems: the jumping, the puzzles, the map exploration, the menus, items, spells, and anything else that makes the gameplay of my game.
This is because I noticed that in several games made in RPG Maker, the combat and the gameplay take a backseat while everyone gushes about the art, music, themes, story, characters, dialogue and sometimes voice acting.
I know there are plenty of commercial, sometimes big-budget RPGs that are beloved mostly because of their narratives and characters, for example most games by Black Isle Studios and Obsidian, but there's definitely a lack of RPG Maker games praised for their combat.
In other words, please use custom combat plugins in your games.
